presentingComplaint: Progressive drowsiness, confusion and twitching over 5 days, brought in by family after he became difficult to rouse.
history: Type 2 diabetes for 18 years and diabetic nephropathy with CKD stage 5 (baseline creatinine ~4.5 mg/dL, eGFR ~12), managed conservatively and not yet on dialysis; also hypertensive. Over the past week he became increasingly lethargic, forgetful and irritable, with reduced appetite, nausea and hiccups. In the last 48 h he has been intermittently disoriented, sleeps most of the day, and the family noticed sudden jerky movements of the hands. Missed his last two nephrology appointments and reduced his fluid output markedly. No fever, no headache, no head trauma, no fall, no focal weakness or slurred speech, no seizure witnessed but brief myoclonic jerks seen. No alcohol use, no new sedatives; metformin was stopped last year, on insulin, amlodipine and a loop diuretic. No jaundice, no prior liver disease.
examination: Drowsy, rousable to voice, disoriented to time and place, GCS 12 (E3V4M5). Coarse flapping tremor (asterixis) of outstretched hands, multifocal myoclonic jerks, and mild generalised hyperreflexia; no lateralising or focal neurological deficit, pupils equal and reactive, no neck stiffness or photophobia, fundi normal. Uraemic fetor noted. Volume-overloaded: mild pitting pedal oedema and raised JVP, chest with bibasal crackles. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no organomegaly, no ascites, no shifting dullness. No asterixis-masking flap of hepatic type on further inspection; no jaundice or spider naevi. Sallow, sallow-grey complexion. Afebrile.

labs.phEnzymes: ABG: pH 7.28, HCO3 13, high anion gap

imaging: Non-contrast CT head: age-related atrophy, no haemorrhage, no infarct, no mass or midline shift, no hydrocephalus. Chest X-ray: mild pulmonary venous congestion. Renal ultrasound: bilateral small echogenic kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation, consistent with chronic parenchymal disease.
microbiology: Not indicated for diagnosis; afebrile with no localising source. Blood cultures and urine culture sent to exclude occult sepsis as a precipitant returned negative; CSF not sampled as clinical picture is metabolic with no meningism and reversible cause identified.
differentialDiagnoses: Hepatic encephalopathy (excluded: no liver disease, normal ammonia/LFTs/INR, no ascites)
Symptomatic hyponatraemia / SIADH (Na only mildly low at 132, insufficient to explain coma)
Drug/sedative intoxication (no ingestion history, though reduced renal drug clearance considered)
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (excluded: near-normal glucose, no marked hyperosmolality)
finalDiagnosis: Uraemic (metabolic) encephalopathy in CKD stage 5 with diabetic nephropathy, precipitated by progressive uraemia, high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and volume overload; an indication for renal replacement therapy.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Acute Confusional States and Encephalopathy
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Chronic Kidney Disease and Uremia
KDIGO - Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease 2024
stewardship: Not applicable - this is a non-infective metabolic encephalopathy. No empiric antimicrobials are indicated; the confusion is driven by uraemia, acidosis and electrolyte derangement, not infection. Sepsis was actively excluded as a reversible precipitant (afebrile, no source, negative cultures) rather than empirically treated, avoiding unnecessary antibiotic exposure. Management is correction of the metabolic derangement and urgent nephrology referral for dialysis initiation.
contraindications: Avoid renally-cleared or sedating drugs (e.g., long-acting benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids, opioids) that accumulate in CKD and worsen encephalopathy
Avoid nephrotoxins and further volume overload; caution with contrast
Do not attribute altered sensorium to sedatives without checking metabolic panel first
Metformin contraindicated at this eGFR (risk of lactic acidosis)
edgeCases: Uraemic and hepatic encephalopathy can coexist and both cause asterixis; a normal ammonia and LFTs point away from hepatic cause here
Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome can paradoxically worsen encephalopathy if uraemia is corrected too rapidly at first session
Severe hyperkalaemia and acidosis can independently depress consciousness and must be corrected in parallel
In diabetics, exclude hypoglycaemia and HHS at the bedside before anchoring on uraemia
expectedMaiK: In a patient with CKD stage 5 and diabetic nephropathy presenting with progressive altered sensorium, asterixis and myoclonus, euglycaemia with markedly elevated urea/creatinine, high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and a structurally normal CT head indicate uraemic (metabolic) encephalopathy - a reversible, dialysis-responsive cause that must not be mistaken for a primary neurological event or empirically treated as infection.
expectedNextQuestions: What is the baseline renal function and last dialysis/nephrology contact, and how rapidly has urea/creatinine risen?
Any new or accumulating renally-cleared/sedating drugs, or missed medications?
Is there any fever or localising symptom suggesting infection as a precipitant?
What is the current urine output and volume status?
Any features of liver disease, and what is the ammonia/LFT profile?
expectedInvestigations: Venous/arterial blood gas with anion gap
Serum electrolytes including sodium, potassium, calcium, phosphate
Serum ammonia and liver function tests
Blood and urine cultures to exclude infective precipitant
